blocks.text: Before a client can call a single tool or read a single resource, it has to go through a startup routine first.
That routine has a fixed shape, create the client, open a connection, shake hands with the server, and only then start real work.
This lesson walks through each step of that routine, the constructor options you will actually configure, and the mistakes that trip up first time client authors.
1. Why Initialization Is Its Own Stage

blocks.alt: Why Initialization Is Its Own Stage
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012815-671045535.png
It is tempting to treat startup as boilerplate you write once and forget.
But a client that skips or rushes initialization ends up talking to a server whose capabilities it never actually confirmed.

blocks.title: Initialization is a contract, not a formality
blocks.content: The initialize handshake is the one moment where client and server agree on what they can do together. Skipping it means guessing instead of knowing.

blocks.text: 2. Step One: Creating a Client Instance
The first step is simply constructing a client object in your host application.
At this point no network or process connection exists yet, you are just building a value in memory.
The name and version here describe your client application, not the server it will eventually talk to.
3. Step Two: Opening a Transport Connection

blocks.alt: Step Two: Opening a Transport Connection
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012815-508528498.png
A client instance on its own cannot talk to anything, it needs a transport.
The transport is the actual pipe, stdio, HTTP, or WebSocket, that carries JSON-RPC messages back and forth.
Calling connect does two things at once, it opens the transport and, under the hood, kicks off the initialize handshake for you.

blocks.title: connect() usually hides the handshake
blocks.content: Most SDKs bundle the initialize request and initialized notification inside the connect call, so you rarely write the JSON-RPC messages by hand. It still helps to know what is happening underneath.

blocks.text: 4. Step Three: Sending the initialize Request

blocks.alt: Step Three: Sending the initialize Request
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012815-549238997.png
Once the transport is open, the client sends an initialize request as the very first message.
This request carries the protocol version the client speaks and the capabilities it supports.
Nothing else should be sent on this connection before this request goes out.
5. Step Four: Receiving the Server Capabilities
The server answers with its own protocol version and the capabilities it actually supports.
This is the moment the client learns whether the server offers tools, resources, prompts, or some combination of those.
A well behaved client stores this response and checks it before assuming any particular feature is available.
6. Step Five: Sending the initialized Notification

blocks.alt: Step Five: Sending the initialized Notification
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012815-478685552.png
After accepting the server response, the client sends back an initialized notification.
A notification carries no id and expects no reply, it is simply the client confirming the handshake is done on its side.
Only after this notification goes out is the connection considered fully live by both sides.
7. Putting the Whole Handshake Together
Here is the same sequence again, but drawn as a decision flow rather than a list of messages.
Notice the branch, a client that finds a protocol version it cannot support should close the connection instead of pushing forward.
8. Typical Client SDK Constructor Options
Most MCP client SDKs expose a small, predictable set of constructor options.
Knowing what each one actually controls saves you from copying boilerplate you do not understand.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Option","What it controls","Typical default"],"rows":[["name","Identifies your client application to the server","No default, required"],["version","Your client application version, useful for server side logging","No default, required"],["capabilities","Which optional client features you support, like sampling or roots","Empty object"],["requestTimeoutMs","How long to wait for a response before failing a request","Varies by SDK"],["transport","Which transport implementation to connect through","Must be provided"]]}

blocks.text: The capabilities object here is easy to underestimate, it is not decoration, it is what the server will check before trying to use a client side feature.
9. Python SDK Equivalent
The same five steps look almost identical in the Python SDK, just wrapped in an async context manager.

code.content:
import asyncio
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

async def main():
    server_params = StdioServerParameters(
        command="python",
        args=["weather_server.py"]
    )

    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read_stream, write_stream):
        async with ClientSession(read_stream, write_stream) as session:
            # this call sends initialize and initialized for you
            await session.initialize()

            tools = await session.list_tools()
            print(tools)

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: Notice the shape matches the TypeScript version exactly, create, connect, initialize, then use.
10. Why Order Matters Here
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012816-299906698.png
Each of the five steps depends on the one before it finishing cleanly.
A transport that is not open yet has nothing to send an initialize request over.
A client that has not received capabilities yet has no basis for deciding what it is safe to call.

blocks.title: Order is not a suggestion
blocks.content: The MCP specification treats this sequence as strict. A server is allowed to reject or ignore requests that arrive out of order, and many implementations do exactly that.

blocks.text: 11. Waiting for the Handshake to Actually Finish
A common trap is calling connect and immediately calling listTools right after, without awaiting the connection properly.
Because connect is asynchronous, code that does not await it can race ahead before the handshake completes.
The fix is almost always this small, but the bug it prevents can be maddening to track down later.
12. What Happens If You Forget initialized

blocks.alt: What Happens If You Forget initialized
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012816-154183753.png
Some hand rolled clients send the initialize request, read the response, and then jump straight into calling tools.
Skipping the initialized notification leaves the server unsure whether the client is actually ready.
Strict server implementations may reject subsequent requests outright until that notification arrives.

blocks.title: This mistake often hides in custom clients
blocks.content: SDK provided connect and initialize helpers send this notification for you automatically. The bug usually only appears in code that implements the handshake by hand.

blocks.text: 13. Handling a Capability Mismatch
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012817-808920222.png
Sometimes the server capabilities that come back do not include something your client was hoping to use.
The right response is to check for a capability before relying on it, not to assume it exists.
This one check prevents a whole category of runtime errors that only show up against a server you have not tested with before.
14. Timeouts and Retries During Startup
A transport connection or an initialize request can hang, especially over a network transport.
Most SDKs let you set a request timeout, and it is worth setting one explicitly rather than trusting a default you have not checked.

items: Set an explicit timeout on the initialize call so a hung server does not block startup forever.
Decide up front whether a failed handshake should retry once or fail immediately and surface an error.
Log the exact stage where startup failed, transport open, initialize sent, or waiting on a response.

Run this against any MCP server and you should see a clean sequence of stage logs, ending with the tool count once the handshake is truly done.
Common Mistakes
A handful of startup mistakes come up again and again in real client code.

items: Calling connect without awaiting it, then immediately calling other client methods.
Forgetting to send the initialized notification when implementing the handshake by hand instead of using an SDK helper.
Assuming a server supports a capability instead of checking the response from initialize.
Never setting a timeout on the initialize request, so a hung server blocks startup indefinitely.
Reusing a client instance across two different transports without creating a fresh connection.
Logging to the same stream the transport uses for protocol messages, which corrupts the handshake on stdio.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the worked example above and point it at a simple local server you have access to.
Add a deliberate bug, remove the await in front of client.connect, and watch what happens to the tool count log.

items: Stretch goal one: add a five second timeout around the initialize call and confirm it fires against a server that never responds.
Stretch goal two: log the full capabilities object returned by the server and compare it against what the server actually implements.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
A client startup is five steps, create the instance, open the transport, send initialize, receive capabilities, and send initialized, always in that order.
Getting this sequence right, and actually waiting for it to finish, is what makes every later tool call and resource read reliable instead of a race.
